questions.question_text: A particle moving in a straight line has acceleration $a = 4t + 3\text{ m/s}^{2}$, and $v = 20\text{ m/s}$ when $t = 2$. What is $v$ as a function of $t$?

options.why: Treated $v = 20$ as the value at $t = 0$, so the constant was set to $20$ instead of substituting $t = 2$.
Integrated $4t$ as $4t^{2}$, forgetting to halve the coefficient.
Integrated $4t$ as $4t^{2}$ and also read the given velocity as the value at $t = 0$.

questions.question_text: A particle has velocity $v = 6t^{2} - 10t + 1\text{ m/s}$, and $x = 3\text{ m}$ when $t = 1$. What is $x$ as a function of $t$?

options.why: Wrote the constant as the given displacement $3$ rather than solving $-2 + c = 3$.
Integrated $-10t$ as $-10t^{2}$, forgetting to halve the coefficient.
Integrated $-10t$ as $-10t^{2}$ and also set the constant equal to the given displacement.

questions.question_text: A particle has constant acceleration $a = -6\text{ m/s}^{2}$, with $v(0) = 12\text{ m/s}$ and $x(0) = 5\text{ m}$. What is $x$ as a function of $t$?

options.why: Swapped the two initial conditions, using $x(0)$ as the initial velocity and $v(0)$ as the initial displacement.
Integrated $-6t$ as $-6t^{2}$ at the second integration instead of $-3t^{2}$.
Integrated $-6t$ as $-6t^{2}$ and also swapped the two initial conditions.

questions.solution_text:
$v = \displaystyle\int -6\,dt$
$= -6t + c$
$\text{When } t = 0,\ v = 12:\ c = 12$
$v = -6t + 12$
$x = \displaystyle\int (-6t + 12)\,dt$
$= -3t^{2} + 12t + d$
$\text{When } t = 0,\ x = 5:\ d = 5$
$x = -3t^{2} + 12t + 5$

questions.question_text: A particle starts at the origin with velocity $v = 3t^{2} - 27\text{ m/s}$ for $t \ge 0$. What is its **displacement** over the first $5$ seconds?

options.why: Gave the distance travelled: the particle turns around at $t = 3$, and the two legs were added instead of taking $x(5) - x(0)$.
Took the size of the answer and dropped the negative sign, but displacement keeps its direction.
Stopped at the turning point $t = 3$ and gave the displacement there rather than at $t = 5$.

questions.solution_text:
$x = \displaystyle\int (3t^{2} - 27)\,dt$
$= t^{3} - 27t + c$
$\text{When } t = 0,\ x = 0:\ c = 0$
$x(5) = 125 - 135$
$= -10\text{ m}$
$\text{Displacement} = x(5) - x(0)$
$= -10\text{ m}$

questions.question_text: A particle moves with $x = t^{2} - 8t + 3$ metres for $0 \le t \le 6$ seconds. What **distance** does it travel over this interval?

options.why: Gave the size of the displacement $x(6) - x(0) = -12$, ignoring that the particle turns around at $t = 4$.
Counted only the first leg, from $t = 0$ to the turning point at $t = 4$.
Counted only the second leg, from the turning point at $t = 4$ to $t = 6$.

questions.question_text: A particle moves with $x = t^{3} - 3t^{2} - 9t + 1$ metres for $t \ge 0$. Which statement about the particle at $t = 2$ is correct?

options.text: It is slowing down, because $v = -9$ and $a = 6$ have opposite signs.
It is speeding up, because the acceleration $a = 6$ is positive.
options.why: Assumes a positive acceleration always means speeding up; speeding up requires $v$ and $a$ to share a sign.

options.text: It is speeding up, because the velocity $v = -9$ is negative and so is becoming more negative.
options.why: Assumes a negative velocity keeps growing in size; here the positive acceleration is pulling the velocity back towards zero.

options.text: It is at rest, because $v = -9$ and $a = 6$ have opposite signs.
options.why: Confuses opposite signs with the particle being at rest; at rest requires $v = 0$.

questions.solution_text:
$v = \dot{x} = 3t^{2} - 6t - 9$
$a = \ddot{x} = 6t - 6$
$v(2) = 12 - 12 - 9$
$= -9\text{ m/s}$
$a(2) = 12 - 6$
$= 6\text{ m/s}^{2}$
$\text{The signs of } v \text{ and } a \text{ are opposite, so the speed } |v| \text{ is decreasing.}$
The particle is slowing down.

questions.question_text: A particle moves with $x = t^{3} - 15t^{2} + 63t$ metres for $t \ge 0$. At which times does the particle change direction?

options.why: Solved $\ddot{x} = 0$, which gives the time the acceleration changes sign, not the velocity.
Solved $x = 0$ instead of $v = 0$; that is the time at the origin, not a change of direction.
Found one root of $3t^{2} - 30t + 63 = 0$ and stopped, missing the second root $t = 7$.

questions.solution_text:
$v = \dot{x} = 3t^{2} - 30t + 63$
$= 3(t - 3)(t - 7)$
$\text{Set } v = 0:$
$t = 3\text{ or } t = 7$
$v(0) = 63 > 0,\ v(5) = -12 < 0,\ v(8) = 15 > 0$
The velocity changes sign at both times, so the particle changes direction at $t = 3$ s and $t = 7$ s.

questions.question_text:
The velocity–time graph of a particle moving in a straight line is shown, where $v = t^{2} - 6t + 5\text{ m/s}$ for $0 \le t \le 6$ seconds.
[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}[every node/.style={font=\large}]
\begin{axis}[axis lines=middle, xlabel={$t$ (s)}, ylabel={$v$ (m/s)},
             xmin=-0.6, xmax=6.8, ymin=-5.5, ymax=6.5,
             xtick={1,2,3,4,5,6}, ytick={-4,-2,2,4,6}, samples=100, clip=false,
             width=10cm, height=8cm]
\addplot[thick, domain=0:6] {x*x - 6*x + 5};
\end{axis}
\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]
During which times is the particle moving in the negative direction?

options.why: Read the parts of the graph above the $t$-axis, which are where the particle moves in the positive direction.
Gave the times at rest, where $v = 0$, instead of the interval on which $v$ is negative.
Read where the graph is falling and treated a decreasing velocity as a negative velocity.

questions.solution_text:
$\text{The particle moves in the negative direction where } v < 0.$
$t^{2} - 6t + 5 = 0$
$(t - 1)(t - 5) = 0$
$t = 1\text{ or } t = 5$
$\text{The parabola is below the } t\text{-axis between its roots.}$
The particle moves in the negative direction for $1 < t < 5$.
